title: what a sikh carries and why
hook: what a Sikh carries and why
tomorrow: the tenth guru, the khalsa, the saint-soldier

segments.voice: Yesterday: chardi kala, ever-rising spirits. Your line was rise anyway. When something went wrong, which way did you face? Day sixteen.

A wedding ring, turned on the finger during a hard meeting. A photo in a wallet. A string tied around a wrist. A grandmother's watch that doesn't even keep time anymore. Small things people carry to remember. They don't do anything, exactly. But touch one, and something comes back: a promise, a person, who someone meant to be. Initiated Sikhs carry five of those, all day, every day, each one tied to something different. Today: what a Sikh carries, and why.
screen: `A RING, A PHOTO, A STRING.` → `TOUCH IT, AND SOMETHING COMES BACK.` → `A SIKH CARRIES FIVE.`

segments.voice: They're called the five Ks, because in Punjabi each one begins with the sound k. Sikhs who have been initiated into the Khalsa, the community of the committed, keep all five. The tradition traces them to the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, whom you'll meet tomorrow. One. Kesh: uncut hair, which you met on day twelve under the turban. Accepting the body as it was made. Two. Kanga: a small wooden comb, tucked into the hair. Keep the hair clean and ordered, and the life too. Three. Kara: a plain steel bracelet on the wrist. A circle, with no beginning and no end, like the one God. Sikhs often say that when your hand reaches for something, the kara is there first, asking: is this something a Sikh's hand should do? Four. Kachera: a cotton undergarment, like simple shorts. Self-restraint, and readiness to move. Five. Kirpan: a small sword, worn in a sheath, often under the clothes. It's a symbol of the duty to protect people who can't protect themselves, and of dignity and courage; it isn't there for aggression. Notice something about all five. None is a decoration. Each is plain, practical, ordinary: a comb, a bracelet, underwear, hair. That's the point. The reminders aren't locked in a temple. They're on the body, all day, at work, in the shower, at the gym. Faith you can touch. And for Sikhs who aren't initiated, the kara especially is widely worn, a single steel circle that says the same thing: remember.
screen: `FIVE THINGS THAT BEGIN WITH K.` · `KESH AND KANGA — HAIR, AND ITS COMB.` · `KARA — THE HAND REMEMBERS.` · `KACHERA AND KIRPAN — RESTRAINT, PROTECTION.` · then, large: `FAITH YOU CAN TOUCH.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you're wearing or carrying right now: a ring, a watch, a hair tie, your sleeve. Put your hand on it. Decide, just for today, what it's going to remind you of: something you believe, a person, a promise. Close your hand around it and breathe with that meaning for a while. Let the object and the reminder become one thing. The bell holds the time.
The five Ks. Kesh, kanga, kara, kachera, kirpan: five reminders a committed Sikh carries every day. Sixteenth word.
Your line: reminders you can touch. Each time you touch the thing you chose today, let it bring its reminder back. Day sixteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs initiated into the Khalsa keep the five Ks at all times: uncut hair, a wooden comb, a steel bracelet, a cotton undergarment and a small sword. Many other Sikhs wear the kara.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: kakar, the name for the five articles of faith that begin with k.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh uniform.
what it means: five plain reminders, worn on the body every day: hair, comb, bracelet, undergarment, sword.
what a scholar hears: in Punjabi they're the panj kakar. the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, lists them as required for initiated Sikhs.
